So, walk me through it. Not the titles — the moments where the job changed underneath you.
There are three. The first was a four-year stint on site, straight out of university, which nobody would call a career move and which taught me how the company actually works.
And the second?
2011. My father got ill and I was thrown in at the deep end. But by then I had already taken on the commercial side, so it was less of a jump than it looks on paper.
What had changed in the company by then?
A great deal. We had completed around thirty buildings, we had lost two of our oldest clients, and nobody had ever written a succession plan. I inherited all three of those on the same afternoon.
And the third moment? Take your time.

2016. We consolidated instead of growing, which felt like a misstep at the time. In hindsight it was the two years that laid the groundwork for everything since. What made you ask about the moments rather than the roles?
Before I took over, nobody had written a succession plan.
In hindsight, taking the fifth project was a misstep.
My predecessor had laid the groundwork long before I arrived.

The year I always get asked about is the one where both founders left within about four months of each other. On paper it looks like a promotion. It was a rescue. And the part nobody sees is that by the time it happened I had already been running the operation for two years without the title, so it was less of a jump than the resume suggests. What I inherited was not glamorous. There was a supplier contract nobody had read in six years, and a team that had lost two managers and had stopped expecting anybody to stay. Nobody had written anything down. Not the pricing logic, not the client history, nothing. In hindsight, the two quiet years before that year are the ones that mattered, because they were the groundwork, and at the time I thought they were the years I was wasting.

Three moves. That is the shape of an answer that works, and most people give me thirteen, one for every job they have ever had, and the listener stops keeping track somewhere around the fourth. Three. And inside each one there has to be a reason. Not what the job was, which is already on the form, but what had happened that made the move necessary or possible. A move without a reason is just a date, and dates are the part I can read for myself. Now, the misstep. Every strong answer I have ever heard has one in it, said without drama, in one sentence, with what it cost. And the candidates who present a career with no wrong turns at all are, without exception, the ones nobody in the room believes. It is not modesty. It is that a clean line is not what twenty years looks like.

Researchers at a European business school did something unusual: they asked around two hundred senior managers to tell their career story, and then asked the same people to tell it again a year later, without showing them the first recording. The second version was consistently different in one direction. It had fewer people in it and more decisions, and the luck had almost entirely disappeared. What gets edited out, the researchers argue, is nearly always the part somebody else set up. A predecessor's groundwork. A market that turned for reasons nobody in the room controlled. The person who handed you the responsibility on a Friday afternoon without a conversation. We spoke to an interviewer at one of the schools involved, who put it more simply. She listens for whether the candidate can name one thing that was not their own doing, because a career with no external force in it, she says, has been edited.
